analysis.one_liner: Lets victims of gun violence sue firearm manufacturers and dealers, ending their special legal shield.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past committee: introduced June 20, 2023, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action before the 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 2005, a federal law called the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act has blocked most lawsuits against gun makers, sellers, importers, dealers, and their trade associations for harms caused when a firearm is criminally or unlawfully misused — a shield no other consumer product industry enjoys. This bill repeals that law, so victims of gun violence could sue the manufacturers, dealers, or trade groups they believe bear responsibility, under ordinary product-liability and negligence rules. It also makes ATF's firearms trace data usable as evidence in civil suits. It never received any action beyond introduction and referral to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Victims of gun violence and their families — including people shot with guns trafficked across state lines, municipalities, and survivors who currently cannot recover damages — would gain the same right to sue negligent companies that consumers of cars, toys, and pharmaceuticals already have. State and local governments burdened by gun violence costs would also be able to bring claims.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun violence victims and their families

how_it_helps.text: Repeals sections 2 through 4 of the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act (15 U.S.C. 7901-7903), which bars civil actions against firearm or ammunition manufacturers, sellers, importers, dealers, and trade associations for damages resulting from criminal or unlawful misuse of a firearm.

Makes the ATF's Firearms Trace System database subject to subpoena and discovery, admissible as evidence, and usable in civil actions in state and federal courts and administrative proceedings, so plaintiffs can use trace data to establish how a crime gun reached the shooter.

analysis.who_pays: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, dealers, importers, sellers, and their trade associations would bear the cost of defending suits and paying judgments, and associated liability-insurance costs would rise. Insurers, and ultimately gun buyers through prices, would absorb part of the cost.

drawbacks.text: Gun makers and dealers would face higher liability exposure for products used illegally by third parties, which could raise costs, reduce sales in some jurisdictions, or prompt defensive changes in distribution; smaller dealers could be hit hardest.

Critics of repealing the 2005 act argue it is the core legal protection for a constitutionally enumerated industry and that reexposing an entire lawful industry to litigation over third-party criminal acts is unfair, whatever its benefits for victims.

The trace-data provision would make law-enforcement data subject to discovery and public use in litigation, which opponents of trace-data openness have long argued could complicate criminal investigations and raise privacy and evidentiary questions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For victims and municipalities, the bill's benefit is large and direct: it removes a liability shield unique to this industry and gives them access to the courts and to evidence they can currently be denied. The cost falls on a specific industry, in litigation risk and insurance, and is partly passed to gun buyers through prices — which is how liability costs are priced into other consumer products. The strongest honest objection is that this re-opens litigation over third-party criminal acts against a lawful industry, which goes beyond how liability is generally assigned in other product sectors; that trade-off is real, but the bill's targeted repeal is narrower than the absolute liability some critics fear, since standard product-liability and negligence defenses would still apply after repeal.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and stayed there — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced June 20, 2023 by Sen. Blumenthal with 26 original Senate cosponsors.
Read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
No further action was taken: no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded before the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.
The bill attracted 29 total cosponsors, all Democrats or independents; no Republican cosponsor ever signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, dealers, and their trade associations are better off: the liability shield that keeps them insulated from most suits over criminal misuse of their products remains fully in force, and the trace-data restrictions on plaintiffs also stay in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun makers, dealers, and trade associations

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and lined up 26 original Senate cosponsors on the day of introduction.

for.name: 28 Democratic senators and 1 independent
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill a full Senate Democratic caucus roster of support but no Republican cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (Chair Dick Durbin, D-IL; ranking member Lindsey Graham, R-SC)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or committee vote on the bill, leaving it to expire at the end of the 118th Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican conference
against.role: Majority-party conference with the power to bring bills to the floor
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and none of the party's leaders moved it toward a floor vote; party control of the floor schedule kept it from ever being considered.

against.name: Firearm industry and its trade associations
against.role: Industry whose liability protections the bill would repeal
against.what_they_did: Long-standing opponents of repealing the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act, which the industry regards as essential protection for a constitutionally enumerated business; the industry lobbied against repeal efforts.

sides.party_line_note: All 29 cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Republican ever signed on, and the bill never reached a vote in the Republican-controlled or Democratic-controlled Senate of the 118th Congress.

industries.note: They are the bill's principal target: repeal of the 2005 act would strip away the liability shield that bars most civil suits against them for criminal or unlawful misuse of their products, exposing them to litigation, judgments, and higher insurance costs. Their interest is directly opposed to that of victims seeking to recover damages.

industries.industry: Gun dealers, retailers, importers, and sellers
industries.note: The repeal covers sellers, importers, and dealers as well as manufacturers, so dealers could be sued for negligent distribution or sales — a risk currently barred by the 2005 act — affecting small dealers and large chains alike.
The 2005 act explicitly shields trade associations from suit; repeal would allow trade groups themselves to be named as defendants in civil actions, a change they have consistently opposed.

Repeal would create a new class of liability for manufacturers, dealers, and trade associations to insure against, raising both demand for coverage and the price of that coverage; the bill neither mandates nor prohibits such insurance.
